# Job 27: Verse-by-verse research notes

**Summary:** The commentaries I read mostly agree on this chapter. Job swears an oath that he is innocent (vv. 1–6). He wishes on his accusers the fate of the wicked and describes the empty hope of the godless (vv. 7–10). Then he describes the "portion" of the wicked man (vv. 13–23). The main dispute is over who speaks vv. 13–23. Many modern scholars think it is Zophar's missing third speech. The older commentators keep it as Job's words. I found no Catholic, Orthodox, prosperity or word-of-faith commentary on this chapter, so those views are left out. I also found little real disagreement between Protestant traditions; the few contrasts are under "Tradition notes" below.

**Search limits:** Pages I read in full are the Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm), Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-27/) and the NET Bible notes (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27). Everything else comes from search-result excerpts. My search and page-reading tools ran out before I reached the remaining sites.

---

## Introduction: who speaks in vv. 13–23?

**The case for Zophar:**
- Coffman reports that Franks and Watson treat 27:7–23 as Zophar's speech. Anderson noted that this device of making the passage the speech of Zophar, "Has enjoyed considerable prestige among scholars for two centuries. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-27.html
- Constable says Rowley regarded this section as Zophar's third speech. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-27.html
- The Layman's Bible Commentary grants that the imagery and the thought are clearly harmonious with Zophar's manner and ideas. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/job-27.html

**The case for Job:**
- Barnes thinks the objections are too strong. All the ancient versions and manuscripts make this a part of the speech of Job. He adds that Job's next speech never replies to such a speech. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/27-13.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the Zophar theory would require two whole verses to have been lost. It reads vv. 11–23 as Job correcting his own earlier overstatements in ch. 24. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- Ellicott says moving the speech to Zophar may gain symmetry but loses dramatic effect. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/27-13.htm
- Constable says the section is consistent with Job's argument in the immediate context (Job 27:7-10) and previously (Job 24:18-25). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/27-17.html

---

## Verse notes

**v. 1**
- Guzik says Job seems to have waited for Zophar, whose turn it was, but the friends stayed silent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-27/
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that the word "parable" (*mashal*) appears earlier only in Balaam's oracles (Num. 23–24). In its view the new word marks this speech as Job's settled judgment, not argument or emotion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- The NET note says *mashal* usually means a proverb but can mean a longer discourse. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown takes the friends' silence as virtually admitting defeat. https://www.ccel.org/j/jfb/jfb/JFB18.htm

**v. 2**
- "As God lives" was the usual oath of pious Israelites. This is Job's first oath. "Taken away my judgment" means God has declined to hear Job's case. (Pulpit) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- NET: by this formula the speaker stakes God's life on the truth of his words. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27
- Guzik quotes Mason: it is jarringly ironic that Job swears by the living God while accusing that God of deserting him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-27/
- Spurgeon (Baptist) preached on this verse in a sermon called *A Vexed Soul Comforted*. His point: if the Almighty can make the soul bitter, he is also almighty to sweeten it. (Quoted by Guzik.) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-27/
- Matthew Henry is more critical: Job had not due reverence when he spake of God as taking away his judgment, and vexing his soul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/27-1.htm
- Benson reads the oath as Job's answer to friends who would not believe him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/27-1.htm

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: this verse is in brackets. Job claims his mind is still sound. The breath God gave Adam (Gen. 2:7) still lets him judge what is right. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- NET explains the two Hebrew words. *Neshamah* is the breath given to Adam, and its range includes conscience. *Ruach* should be rendered "breath" here because it is in the nostrils. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27
- Coffman reads the verse as a declaration that Job is speaking by the Spirit of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/27-1.html

**v. 4**
- NET: v. 4 is the actual content of the oath. The verb in the second line implies no deceit at all, however quiet or subtle. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27
- Pulpit: confessing guilt, as the friends wanted, would be both wicked and false. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-27.html
- Guzik quotes Trapp: Job complains of God's severity but does not blaspheme. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-27/

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: Job will not admit that his sufferings come from secret sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- NET: "far be it from me" is very strong, close to calling it sacrilege. The "you" is plural, meaning all three friends. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27
- Guzik quotes Andersen, who reads the phrase as a formula of self-cursing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-27/
- Matthew Henry, citing Hebrews 6:16, sees Job confirming his integrity with an oath to end the argument. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_027.cfm
- BibleHub Study Bible: His integrity does not mean sinless perfection, but wholehearted devotion to God and refusal to live dishonestly before Him. https://biblehub.com/job/27-5.htm

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: Job will defend his past life and keep living the same way. That means he will not "curse God, and die." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- Barnes: Job holds on to his awareness that he has been sincere. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/27-6.htm
- NET: "heart" here means conscience. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27
- Several sources take the last line differently: "my heart reproaches none of my days," meaning Job's whole past life. (Maurer, Cambridge, Geneva.) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/27-6.htm
- See also the Gill and Luther notes under "Tradition notes" below.

**v. 7**
- Pulpit is unsure how this verse connects to what comes before. Some read it as a curse on false friends. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- Guzik quotes Andersen: in Israelite law a malicious accuser received the penalty of the crime he falsely charged. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-27/
- NET: Job means like the wicked when they are judged, not when they prosper. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27
- Constable reads it as Job placing himself with the righteous and his opponents with the wicked. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-27.html

**v. 8**
- Clarke says "hypocrite" (KJV) is a poor translation. The word means a wicked fellow, a defiled, polluted wretch. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-27.html
- Pulpit says Job assumes the soul goes on existing after death, and links the verse to Mark 8:36. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- Poole and Benson read Job as claiming a hope of a blessed immortality after death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/27-8.htm
- NET: "cut off" is best read intransitively. One scholar proposed changing the verb to "when he prays." The verb for "takes away" occurs only here and its meaning is disputed. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27
- Douay-Rheims (Catholic translation) renders the verse differently: if through covetousness he take by violence, and God deliver not his soul? https://biblehub.com/job/27-8.htm

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: knowingly living a lie cuts a person off from God and makes prayer useless until it is repented of. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- Guzik: Job agrees God does not hear the hypocrite. Yet Job himself has to endure God's silence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-27/

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: the hypocrite cannot delight in God. Over time his prayer stops or becomes mere habit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- Guzik quotes Poole: the hypocrite gives up when answers are slow, while Job keeps praying. That is evidence Job is no hypocrite. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-27/
- Keil and Delitzsch: Job knows he has a God who does not leave him unheard, in whom he delights himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/27-8.htm

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: this introduction prepares for Job to correct his earlier, overstated claims. "What is with the Almighty" means God's principles of action. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- Guzik: the friends knew true principles but applied them wrongly to Job. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-27/
- NET: "power" is literally "hand." The plural "you" supports the view that Job is addressing the friends. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27

**v. 12**
- NET: the Hebrew piles up the word for vapor ("become vain with vanity"). The Greek Old Testament (LXX) reads "adding vanity to vanity." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27
- Pulpit: the friends have seen God's ways at work but draw the wrong conclusions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm

**v. 13**
- Job deliberately takes up Zophar's own words from 20:29 and grants that they are generally true. (Pulpit) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- Ellicott: Job may be showing he accepts the friends' facts although he will not admit their inferences. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/27-13.htm
- Guzik quotes Andersen: the disagreement is not over whether God is just, but over how his justice works out in particular events. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-27/
- Gill (Baptist) says the wicked man's portion is Not to be punished in this life, but after death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/27-13.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Job is stating Zophar's argument rather than his own. https://www.ccel.org/j/jfb/jfb/JFB18.htm

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: in ch. 21 Job named many children as a sign of the wicked man's prosperity. Here he admits that such children often fall by the sword or end up in poverty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- NET: "bread" means food in general. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27

**v. 15**
- NET: "buried by death" means buried by plague, much as English speaks of "the Black Death." The LXX reads "their widows." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27
- Pulpit: the dead are forgotten, and the widows' failure to mourn would have been a serious shame in that culture. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm

**v. 16**
- Pulpit compares Tyre heaping up silver like dust (Zech. 9:3). The stored clothing may be robes of honour kept to give to guests. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm

**v. 17**
- Pulpit: when the wicked man dies, his goods pass to the just. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel): the wicked may store it up, but someone else will wear it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/27-8.html

**v. 18**
- The moth stands for fragility. Pulpit suggests Job may have had the cocoon in mind. A watchman's hut was the flimsiest kind of shelter (Isa. 1:8). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- NET: some read "spider's web" (the LXX has both moth and spider), and some read "nest." A "booth" is a flimsy shelter. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27
- Guzik quotes Poole: the moth is suddenly brushed off and crushed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-27/

**v. 19**
- NET: the Hebrew reads "not gathered." Many follow the LXX and Syriac: "he will do so no more." Scholars are split on whether "he is not" means the man dies (Gordis, Dhorme) or his wealth vanishes (RSV, ESV, NLT). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27
- Pulpit gives similar options. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm

**v. 20**
- Pulpit: the wicked man fears his victims' revenge, losing his wealth and God's final judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- NET: some scholars change "like waters" to "by day" to match "in the night." The NET keeps "waters," which can stand for disaster. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27
- Matthew Henry: death is like a fair gale of wind carrying the godly home, but a storm to the wicked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/27-13.htm

**v. 21**
- Pulpit identifies the east wind as the hot, violent desert wind (the khamsin). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm

**v. 22**
- KJV supplies "God" as the one who casts upon him. Others make the storm the subject. Pulpit says the difference is small, because the storm stands for God's judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- NET translates it as the wind hurling itself without pity. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27

**v. 23**
- NET: if the wind is still the subject, this is bold personification. Others read "men clap" (Gordis). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=27
- Pulpit: people applaud God's judgment and hiss the man's downfall. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/27.htm
- Guzik quotes Clarke: clapping and hissing was an ancient way of driving a disgraced official from office. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-27/
- Guzik: the picture in vv. 13–23 resembles Job's own suffering. Job is not admitting guilt but conceding that his situation looks like judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-27/

---

## Tradition notes (only where I found something)

- **v. 2, Baptist and Presbyterian:** Spurgeon (Baptist) draws comfort from the verse, while Matthew Henry (Presbyterian) faults Job's lack of reverence. These are different emphases, not opposing doctrines. Links are under v. 2 above.
- **v. 6, Baptist/Calvinist:** Gill insists that "my righteousness" is not his personal righteousness, or the righteousness of his works, as his justifying righteousness before God. He says it means the rightness of Job's cause, and it does not claim Job was sinless. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/27-6.htm
- **v. 6, Lutheran:** The Cambridge Bible says these words answer the friends' specific charges, not the sinfulness common to all people. It cites Luther's translation, "My conscience bites me not in respect of my whole life." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/27-6.htm
- **Methodist:** Wesley's Notes outline the chapter as Job's integrity, his dread of hypocrisy, and the miserable end of the wicked, notwithstanding their long prosperity. I only saw the outline, not his notes on each verse. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-job/
